newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark closes off in U.S., dlr/yen steady.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark closes off in U.S., dlr/yen steady.

text.p: The dollar was steady against the yen but closed one pfennig lower against the mark after traders squared stale dollar positions before Federal Reserve policy makers meet on Tuesday.
Activity was very light, with dealers seeking to minimize risk before closing their books for the year.
With so many buyers keeping a low profile on the sidelines, the dollar fell swiftly below 1.5500 marks as traders covered short mark positions.
"People are still digesting the EU stabity pact," said John McCarthy of ING Barings Capital Markets.

"In general, people are feeling it's a weakish one, which should be positive for the dollar in the short-run. But I think the longs on dollar/mark ... were a bit disappointed that they didn't get follow-through," he added.
The dollar fell to 1.5445/55 marks from 1.5545/55 at the open, but after holding above 114 yen for most of the session, the dollar closed at 113.80/90, yen down from 113.88/93.

Despite dollar/mark's sharp fall, traders said it was hard to get a handle on trade, with few fresh factors and general unwillingness to give away any of the year's profits on the off chance of a Fed surprise on Tuesday.
"You'll have a tough time putting much of a spin on anything seen today," said John Beerling, chief dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
"(The Fed meeting) is going to serve to keep us quiet for a little while ...We're looking for no change -- pretty much a steady monetary policy," he added.
The Fed has not altered interest rates since February, when it lowered the discount and Fed funds rates.
Mark/yen surged but closed below its high of 73.87 versus the yen on Monday after opening at 73.18. But against the dollar the yen climbed back from early losses.
Traders said the yen initially weakened amid reduced fears that Japan's appetite for U.S. assets this year, which helped spur the dollar to 42-month highs in October, was eroding.

Last week, convulsed with doubts over whether Japanese investors would sustain their record levels of U.S. bond purchases, Wall Street questioned the longevity of the dollar's recent advance against the yen.

But after steadying, the dollar got an additional boost from an article in the Wall Street Journal on Monday saying Japanese fund managers still have a healthy appetite for, and may even increase buying of, U.S. bonds.

"People are sort of looking for reasons why dollar/yen just won't go down," said Anne Pankowski, vice president of foreign exchange at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, in New York. "You can keep pointing to the fact that there is this seemingly fundamental shift in (Japanese) pension funds offshore."
In addition, the dollar got a morning boost from expectations of heavy demand by Japanese funds for U.S. Treasury notes at this week's auction.
The dollar ignored the higher-than-expected 0.9 percent rise in November U.S. industrial production.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.3190/00 Swiss francs from 1.3280/90 Swiss at the open. It rose to Canadian $1.3669/74 from C$1.3634/39. The pound rose to $1.6658/68 from $1.6585/95.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7925/30, compared to $0.7929/34 at the open.
-- Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667
